entry: American television sitcom (1994–2004). Created by David Crane and Marta Kauffman, *Friends* aired on [[NBC]] from September 22, 1994, to May 6, 2004, over ten seasons. The ensemble cast included [[Jennifer Aniston]], [[Courteney Cox]], [[Lisa Kudrow]], Matt LeBlanc, [[Matthew Perry]] and David Schwimmer. Its six friends in their 20s and early 30s live in [[Manhattan]], New York City. The finale drew around 52.5 million American viewers. The series spawned the spin-off *Joey* and the 2021 reunion special *Friends: The Reunion*.

Horse breed originating in Friesland, northern [[Netherlands]]. The Friesian is black with no white markings, typically stands 15 to 16 hands (152 to 163 cm) at the withers, and is used for riding and driving. It is known for a brisk, high-stepping trot and a long, flowing mane and tail. The breed nearly became extinct on more than one occasion. In medieval times Friesians were used to carry knights to battle. About 0.25% of Friesians are affected by [[Dwarfism|dwarfism]], a recessive condition. The breed also has acknowledged disorders including hydrocephalus, a tendency for aortic rupture and megaesophagus. The relatively small gene pool and [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]] are thought to be factors behind most of these disorders.

Type of warship. In the 17th to early 18th centuries the term was loosely applied to any full-rigged ship built for speed and maneuverability and intended for scouting, escort or patrol. The "true frigate", developed in France in the second quarter of the 18th century, had a single gun deck of 28 and 36 cannons. The term was reintroduced in the [[World War II|Second World War]] for a seagoing escort between a [[Corvette|corvette]] and a [[Destroyer|destroyer]]. Since then it has covered anti-submarine warfare ships, corvettes, destroyers and nuclear-powered guided-missile cruisers.

Family of [[Seabird|seabirds]] (*Fregatidae*). The five living species, all in the genus *Fregata*, range across tropical and subtropical oceans. Males are mostly black with a red gular pouch that they inflate in the breeding season to attract females; females have white underbellies. Frigatebirds have the largest wing area to body mass ratio of any bird, and their wings span up to 2.3 meters (7.5 ft). They soar for weeks on wind currents and catch fish and squid that predators such as [[Tuna|tuna]] drive to the surface. They are kleptoparasites that sometimes rob other seabirds of food, and they breed only every other year. Two species, the [[Christmas Island]] and [[Ascension Island]] frigatebirds, are endangered. The oldest fossils date to the early [[Eocene]], around 50 million years ago.

Inquiries far outside mainstream science. The term describes ideas that are highly speculative or rely on premises already refuted, and it covers everything from novel hypotheses testable by the [[Scientific method|scientific method]] to wild ad hoc hypotheses and mumbo jumbo. The boundary between fringe science and [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]] is disputed. Some concepts once accepted by mainstream science later became fringe after re-evaluation. Focal infection theory was considered medical fact, but it was dismissed for lack of evidence. Continental drift was rejected for decades before [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] was accepted.

Gliding toy or sporting item, also called a flying disc. Typically made of injection-molded plastic and roughly 20 to 25 centimeters (8 to 10 in) in diameter, it has an airfoil cross-section that reduces [[Drag (physics)|drag]] and increases lift. Spinning the disc stabilizes it, allowing accurate aim and long throws. The longest recorded throw, by David Wiggins Jr., covered 338 meters (1,109 ft). Walter Frederick Morrison and his future wife Lucile began tossing a popcorn can lid after a Thanksgiving Day dinner in 1937. Morrison designed the Pluto Platter in 1955 and sold the rights to Wham-O in 1957, and that June the company gave the disc the brand name Frisbee. Because Frisbee is a registered trademark, organized sports such as ultimate and disc golf avoid the word.

German chemist. Haber won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the [[Haber process]], which synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gas. The process underpins large-scale production of fertilizers and explosives, and an estimated third of annual global food production uses its ammonia. With [[Max Born]], Haber also proposed the Born–Haber cycle for evaluating the lattice energy of an ionic solid. During [[World War I]] he pioneered the use of chlorine and other poisonous gases and is called the father of chemical warfare. Zyklon B, developed from his work without his direct involvement, was used to kill more than 1 million Jews in gas chambers during [[The Holocaust|the Holocaust]]. Haber resigned after the Nazis came to power in 1933. He died of heart failure in a hotel in [[Basel]] while traveling to take up a directorship in [[Mandatory Palestine]].

Austrian-born film director. Lang worked in Germany and later in the United States. His science-fiction film *Metropolis* (1927) and the early film noir *M* (1931) are among his best-known works. His 1929 film *Woman in the Moon* showcased a multi-stage [[Rocket|rocket]] and pioneered the rocket-launch countdown clock. Born in [[Vienna]], he served in the Austrian army in [[World War I]]. Lang fled Nazi Germany in 1933 after a meeting with Propaganda Minister [[Joseph Goebbels|Joseph Goebbels]], who had offered him a position in the state film industry. In Hollywood he directed *Fury* (1936) and *The Big Heat* (1953). He became a naturalized United States citizen in 1939 and returned to Germany in the late 1950s.

Tailless [[Amphibian|amphibian]] of the order *Anura*. Frogs are widely distributed from the tropics to subarctic regions, with the greatest species diversity in [[Tropical rainforest|tropical rainforest]] and [[Wetland|wetland]] areas. They account for around 88% of living amphibian species. The oldest fossil proto-frog, *Triadobatrachus*, comes from the Early Triassic of Madagascar, about 250 million years ago. Most frogs spawn in water, and their [[Tadpole|tadpoles]] [[Metamorphosis|metamorphose]] into semiaquatic adults. Adults generally eat small invertebrates, especially insects, which they catch with an adhesive tongue. Frogs are an important food source for other predators. More than one third of species are considered threatened with extinction, and over 120 are believed to have become extinct since the 1980s. An emerging fungal disease, chytridiomycosis, has spread around the world.

Layer of ice on a solid surface, formed directly from [[Water vapor|water vapor]]. Frost forms when air contains more water vapor than it can normally hold at a specific temperature, so the excess deposits onto nearby surfaces as ice crystals without crossing through a liquid state. The temperature at which this happens is the [[Dew point|dew point]]. Frost is similar to dew but forms below the freezing point of water. Crystal shape depends on temperature, air pressure, air motion, surface roughness and the level of supersaturation. In [[Temperate climate|temperate climates]] frost usually appears on surfaces near the ground as fragile white crystals. Plants that evolved in warmer climates suffer frost damage when water freezes in their cells, so farmers in affected regions often protect their crops.

Injury to skin or other tissue that is allowed to freeze. It most often affects the fingers, toes, nose, ears, cheeks and chin, and it is commonly preceded by frostnip, a paling or reddening that tingles or feels numb. Injury results from ice crystals and blood clots in small blood vessels after thawing. Risk factors include prolonged cold exposure, drinking alcohol, [[Smoking|smoking]] and previous cold injury. Severity is classed as superficial (first and second degree) or deep (third and fourth degree). Treatment is rewarming in water near body temperature, and rapid heating is avoided. [[Ibuprofen|Ibuprofen]] and tetanus toxoid are recommended for pain and swelling, and [[Amputation|amputation]] is sometimes necessary. Evidence of frostbite appears in a pre-Columbian mummy from the Andes. Its first formal description, in 1813, came from Dominique Jean Larrey, a physician in [[Napoleon]]'s army during the invasion of Russia.

Frozen dessert, usually made with yogurt as its main ingredient. It is similar in composition to [[Ice cream|ice cream]], with milk or a milk substitute as its primary base. The mixture is fermented with yogurt cultures, flavored, frozen with air introduced, and served as soft serve or hardened for scooping. Branded frozen yogurt became popular in the [[United States]] in the 1980s as a lower-fat alternative to ice cream. Regulation varies: the Netherlands requires at least 70% yogurt content, while Australia requires at least 45%. Vegan and [[Halal|halal]] varieties are also sold.

Simple ketonic monosaccharide found in many plants. A white, water-soluble solid, fructose is one of the three most common dietary monosaccharides, along with [[Glucose|glucose]] and galactose. It occurs in honey, tree and vine fruits, berries and most root vegetables, and it is often bound to glucose in [[Sucrose|sucrose]]. Fructose is the sweetest of all naturally occurring carbohydrates, with a relative sweetness roughly twice that of glucose. French chemist Augustin-Pierre Dubrunfaut discovered it in 1847. [[Yeast|Yeast]] ferments it to [[Ethanol|ethanol]] and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Fructose undergoes the [[Maillard reaction|Maillard reaction]] more rapidly than glucose because it exists to a greater extent in open-chain form.

Preparations of fruit whose main preserving agent is sugar, sometimes with acid. Stored in glass jars and used as a [[Condiment|condiment]] or spread, they come in many varieties. Sweet preserves such as jams, jellies and marmalades are often eaten at breakfast or in pastries. Savory, acidic preserves made from vegetable fruits such as tomato or [[Zucchini|zucchini]] accompany cheese, cold meats and curries. Jam may be made with or without added water. Low-pectin fruits such as strawberries may be combined with high-pectin fruit such as orange, or given added pectin, citric acid or [[Citrus|citrus]] peel. Preserves contain pieces of fruit, while jams in some regions do not. Korean *cheong* and Afrikaans *konfyt* are regional variants.

Method of cooking food in oil or animal fat. Frying is believed to have first appeared in Ancient Egypt around 2500 BC, when tiger nut cakes were fried in oil. When food contacts oil heated to 150–200 °C (302–392 °F), its water reaches boiling point and vaporizes, forming a crisp crust that protects the center from further oil absorption. The crust browns through caramelization and the [[Maillard reaction|Maillard reaction]], while the starch gelatinizes. Deep frying submerges food in hot oil so that all sides cook at once; [[French fries|French fries]] and tempura are common examples. Sautéing tosses food over high heat in a small amount of oil. Air fryers use only a little oil and are generally considered healthier, with fewer [[Calorie|calories]] and less fat.

Conditions for switching the order of integration in a double integral. The theorem states that if a function is Lebesgue integrable on a rectangle, the double integral equals the iterated integral in either order, so it can be computed one variable at a time. It is named after Guido Fubini, who proved a general result in 1907. Special cases were known earlier, such as through Cavalieri's principle, which was used by [[Leonhard Euler|Leonhard Euler]]. Tonelli's theorem, introduced by Leonida Tonelli in 1909, applies to non-negative measurable functions. The Fubini and Tonelli theorems are usually combined as the Fubini–Tonelli theorem.

Material used to create heat and energy. A fuel is any material that can react with other substances to release energy as [[Heat|thermal energy]] or for work. The concept first applied to chemical energy but now includes nuclear energy from [[Nuclear fission|fission]] and [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]]. Fuels can drive a heat engine, or supply warmth, cooking and industrial processes. Hydrocarbons are by far the most common fuels used by humans. The first known use of fuel was firewood burned by [[Homo erectus|Homo erectus]] nearly two million years ago. After the [[Steam engine|steam engine]] was developed in the United Kingdom in 1769, [[Coal|coal]] came into wider use during the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]]. In 2005 coal provided 40% of the world's electrical power supply. The trend has since moved toward renewable fuels such as [[Biofuel|biofuels]].

[[Counterpoint|Contrapuntal]] composition in two or more voices built on a recurring subject. The word comes from Latin *fuga*, meaning flight or escape. The subject is introduced in imitation in each voice during the exposition. Episodes and further entries of the subject then alternate, usually ending with the subject in the tonic key. A stretto occurs where the subject overlaps itself in different voices. The fugue was a popular technique in the [[Baroque|Baroque]] era, when it showed mastery of harmony and tonality. [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Johann Sebastian Bach]] wrote many, including *The Well-Tempered Clavier*. Later composers such as [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Mozart]], [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Beethoven]] and [[Dmitri Shostakovich|Shostakovich]] also wrote fugues. Because composers decide most structural elements, the fugue is closer to a style of composition than a structural form.

Province in southeast [[China|China]] on the [[Taiwan Strait|Taiwan Strait]]. Its capital is [[Fuzhou|Fuzhou]]. The province's name combines the city names of Fuzhou and Jianzhou, now Nanping. Most of the population identifies as Han, but Fujian is one of China's most culturally and linguistically diverse provinces. The [[Min Chinese|Min]] dialects are most common, and [[Hakka Chinese|Hakka Chinese]] is also spoken. Because of emigration, much of the ethnic Chinese population of [[Taiwan|Taiwan]], Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines speaks Southern Min. In 2022 its GDP reached CN¥5.31 trillion, 8th nationwide. Two of its cities ranked by scientific research output in 2023: [[Xiamen|Xiamen]] 38th and Fuzhou 45th in the world.

Designated city in [[Kyushu|Kyushu]], Japan, and capital of Fukuoka Prefecture. Built along the shores of Hakata Bay, it has been a center of international commerce since ancient times. It is the nearest point among Japan's main islands to the Asian mainland, and it has long been considered the gateway to the country. Its distance from [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] and [[Osaka|Osaka]] helped it develop a distinctive local culture and dialect. Interaction with the [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]] of China was recorded as early as AD 57, when an envoy received a gold seal. The city was designated by government ordinance on April 1, 1972. In July 2011 it passed Kyoto in population, the first city west of the Kansai region to do so since Kyoto was founded in 794.

Nuclear accident at the Fukushima Daiichi plant, Japan, 2011. It began on March 11, 2011, after the Tōhoku earthquake and [[Tsunami|tsunami]] caused electrical grid failure and damaged most backup power, so reactors could not be cooled after shutdown. The [[United Nations|United Nations]] Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation regards it as the worst nuclear incident since [[Chernobyl disaster|Chernobyl]]. It found no adverse health effects among residents attributable to radiation. At least 164,000 residents were displaced, and the displacement is linked to at least 51 deaths. The evacuation was accused of causing more harm than it prevented. Investigations faulted lapses in safety and oversight.

Senegambian language of West and Central Africa. Spoken as a first language by the Fula people from Senegambia and [[Guinea|Guinea]] to [[Cameroon|Cameroon]], [[Nigeria|Nigeria]] and Sudan, it is also called Fulfulde, Pulaar or Fulani. It is spoken by around 36.8 million people across some 18 countries. Fula belongs to the Atlantic branch of Niger–Congo and, unlike most Niger–Congo languages, has no tones. It is a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] in several countries, including Guinea, Senegal and Gambia. Its robust noun class system, with 24 to 26 classes common across dialects, is marked by suffixes on nouns. It was historically written in the Ajami script, an Arabic-based adaptation, while the Latin alphabet is now predominant in education and media.

1987 war film directed by [[Stanley Kubrick|Stanley Kubrick]]. Adapted from Gustav Hasford's novel *The Short-Timers*, the film follows Marine recruits through boot camp at Parris Island, [[South Carolina|South Carolina]], under the abusive drill instructor Gunnery Sergeant Hartman. The second half follows Marines in the [[Tet Offensive|Tet Offensive]] in [[Da Nang|Da Nang]] and [[Huế|Huế]] during the [[Vietnam War|Vietnam War]]. Released by Warner Bros. in 1987, it grossed $120 million against a budget of $16.5–30 million and received positive reviews. It earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay.

Lunar phase with the entire near side sunlit as seen from Earth. It occurs when Earth lies between the [[Sun|Sun]] and the [[Moon|Moon]], roughly once a month. A synodic month averages about 29.53 days. Because of irregularities in the Moon's orbit, new and full moons may fall up to thirteen hours either side of their mean. Full moons are associated with festivals such as Vesak in [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] and Purnima observances in [[Hinduism|Hinduism]]. Folklore links full moons with insomnia and madness, but scientific studies have not found consistent evidence of behavioral effects.

Punctuation mark (.) used mainly to end a declarative sentence. Called a period in North American English, it is also used after many abbreviations and after letters in some initialisms such as U.S. In computing it is called a dot. Its origins lie in a three-dot system introduced in [[Alexandria|Alexandria]] in the 3rd century BCE by Aristophanes of Byzantium. The name period is first attested in [[Old English|Old English]]. By the time [[Printing|printing]] began in Western Europe, the low dot had become the standard form. In the English-speaking world the same mark serves as the decimal separator.
